Les femmes hispaniques à l’écran aux Éta: Hispanic Women on Screen in the U.S. and Quebec: A Greater Presence Behind the Camera Is Needed
Le Québec sait-il mettre en lumière les: Does Quebec know how to showcase Latina women on the big screen without stereotyping them? And is the United States doing any better on this front?
Fatima Lopez au Café des Arts. La jeune: Fatima Lopez at Café des Arts. The young actress hopes to find more audition opportunities in Toronto, where she will soon be moving. Photo credit: Nayeli Chavez
J’ai proposé ce sujet parce que, plus je: I proposed this topic because, when I was younger, I would turn on the TV after school and simply not see any Latinas on Quebec shows. I didn’t see myself. At first, I wanted to write an article about how Latinas are hypersexualized in the media, but I realized the subject was already widely covered in the United States, our neighbours to the south. I decided to focus on our province after talking about it with the screenwriter you’ll read about below. Enjoy the read!
<strong>Au Québec et aux États-Unis, les: In Quebec and the United States, roles written for Hispanic women sometimes reflect reality poorly, in small and large television and film production companies alike. Despite a positive evolution in the characters written for these women, criticism of the stereotypes put forward on screen has persisted over time. We spoke with Fatima, an emerging actress; Carolina*, a screenwriter; and Zaira, a researcher and associate professor at Université de Montréal, to discuss what they have observed within the industry.
Une veste en laine bleue et verte est ac: A blue and green wool jacket hangs on a chair at Café des Arts. Yet summer is well underway, at the beginning of July. The jacket is waiting for its owner, Fatima Lopez, who has arranged to meet us here. On one of the four walls surrounding the customers hang acrylic paintings signed by Enriqueta Ahrensburg. Fatima comes back, picks up her jacket, and we move to a larger table just behind.
Âgée de 25 ans et actrice de profession,: She is 25 years old and an actress by profession. She was born in Buenos Aires, Argentina. After several trips back and forth between the Argentine capital and Montréal, she and her family settled permanently in Montréal in 2016. Having grown up in the city’s West End, the young woman enrolled at John Abbott College, a CEGEP, in its English-language theatre performance program, before completing training at the National Theatre School of Canada.
Nous l’interrogeons sur ses expériences: We ask her about her experiences as an actress since 2021. She pulls her phone out of her pocket and opens up a gold mine: in an Excel document, she has recorded every role she has auditioned for since last year, along with descriptions of all the characters she has played. A colour code identifies the roles she has played for the small or big screen. From what she has observed, French-language series lean more toward a seductive portrayal of Hispanic women. “I realized that for [Canadian] series in English, there were fewer descriptions like fiery, seductive. It was more in [English-Canadian] films that the adjectives kept coming up: strong, tough, stubborn, fiery,” says the young actress, clenching her fist to illustrate her words.
Selon Fatima, les places assignées aux f: According to Fatima, the places assigned to Latin American women on the small screen are marked by a certain fetishism: a Hispanic accent, pronounced curves, and so on. This stereotype, that of the sexy woman, doesn’t reflect reality, she explains. “It bothers me when someone says ‘Latinas’ to talk about [girls with an accent and curves],” sums up Fatima, whose face lights up as she describes her experiences. “Latinas come in all shapes, genders and types!”
Elle pointe son cellulaire, posé sur la: She points to her cellphone, lying on the table, and to the file she has kept up to date since 2024. “Out of all the auditions I’ve done for Latino characters, only one was written by a Latina,” she says, visibly annoyed. “That’s where the stereotypes come from: if someone who isn’t from our culture writes the characters, they’ll have a different perspective. I’m not saying I don’t want Caucasian, Black or Asian people to write roles for us [...], but we need diversity on set, not just in front of the cameras!”
Ses voyages fréquents entre l’Amérique L: Her frequent travels between Latin America and North America immersed her in very different cinematic worlds. Back then, to her, Argentine films weren’t as “cool as American films.” She didn’t watch works from her country of origin. “It kept me from having an Argentine influence. We have really good actors, a lot of talent, but I didn’t watch them because I wanted to be an American [Caucasian] actress,” she explains. “When I watched TV, it was mostly Caucasian women who had the lead.”
C’est l’émission <em>Les sorciers de Wav: It was the show Wizards of Waverly Place, where the main characters are Italian-Mexican, that made her realize it was possible for her to become an actress without denying her origins.
Quelques jours plus tard, nous retrouvon: A few days later, we meet Carolina, a screenwriter. On Avenue Henri-Julien in Montréal is one of the entrances to Marché Jean-Talon, which welcomes its visitors on this July day when the sun is beating down. A trio of birds lands on the ground and hops toward a pie vendor’s counter, before taking off toward another aisle of the market. Carolina joins us at one of the raised tables at the entrance, sheltered by the ceiling. Her braided hair pulls back from her face. Under her arm, a large carton of eggs she has just bought hides her handbag, striped in black, orange, pink and green. We meet her after asking her a few questions over the phone about the subject that interests us. Her perspective as an experienced Latin American screenwriter helps us understand the power that film and television production teams hold during pre-production.
Son constat est sans appel : elle observ: Her assessment is unequivocal: she observes that in Quebec, roles conceived for Hispanic women often portray them as humiliated women or women going through great suffering. Even in the 90s, the small supporting roles that Latin American women played were cleaning ladies, mothers weeping for their sons at the courthouse, or assault victims, Carolina explains.
Carolina est tout de même consciente des: Carolina is nonetheless aware of the limits that some production teams may face. “It’s very hard to write for cultures you don’t necessarily come into contact with every day,” she concedes, her eyes fixed on the ceiling… “If the only Latina in your circle is a cleaning lady, that’s what you’re going to write.”
Les mains de Carolina. Elle garde espoir: Carolina’s hands. She remains hopeful for the future. Photo credit: Nayeli Chavez
La création des fiches de personnages ne: The creation of character sheets doesn’t come from bad intentions, she says, but from a lack of imagination: “There’s a snobby woman from Westmount who comes to criticize the main character because she thinks he’s being impolite in a restaurant. Why couldn’t she be Latina? She’s never Latina. The snob is going to be white; it’s associated with a social class,” Carolina observes.
Sa tresse tombe sur ses épaules et ses d: Her braid falls over her shoulders and her fingers run along her hair. “I’d love to see [us] in other social classes, to be the motivating teacher who inspires her student in French class, for example. Seeing [Latina women] in other roles in society would be really empowering,” the screenwriter maintains. “[...] These positive role models are very important for young people.”
Carolina compare la situation avec le mo: Carolina compares the situation to the world of theatre, a field in which she also works. Before Quebecers, it was the French who trod the boards. “It’s when Quebecers started seeing themselves on stage that they recognized themselves as a people.” Her hands move in front of her white tank top, backing up her words. “That’s why it’s important to see people from different cultures be part of the reality on television. That’s how we include them in our society: it’s by seeing themselves [that they’ll tell themselves] they’re part of our culture.”
Carolina évoque la série états-unienne B: Carolina brings up the American series Brooklyn Nine-Nine, adapted in Quebec in 2020. A controversy followed: in the original series, two detectives are played by Stephanie Beatriz, who was born in Argentina, and Melissa Fumero, the daughter of a Cuban couple. “It’s a perfect example: they’re Latina women, cops, top of their class, super smart, a little ‘awkward’... they’re really fantastic characters, with lots of nuance, who aren’t defined at all by their Latina origins,” Carolina explains.
Mais la production québécoise a choisi M: But the Quebec production chose Mylène Mackay and Bianca Gervais, actresses who are not Latina, to play the two detectives. “[The writers] said there were a lot more Latinos in the United States than here, and that they were trying to represent [Quebec] reality. I can understand that, it’s not the same reality,” Carolina explains. In 2020, the population of New York City was in fact nearly<l1> 27% Hispanic</l1>, compared with<l2> 1.6% in Quebec City</l2> in 2021.
Même si de nombreuses critiques se sont: Even though many criticisms were voiced in Quebec and the United States following this change to the script, this performing arts enthusiast notes an improvement in the province when it comes to the representation of diversity in film and television. “Right now, we’re figuring out how to make it organic and true, but we’re [in Quebec] in the ‘awkward’ phase of adolescence, where it’s not a finished product yet. There’s still a lot of clumsiness, but the will is there, we’ve moved forward on the path, we mustn’t forget that,” Carolina reminds us.
Le temps file, elle doit bientôt partir: Time is flying; she has to leave soon for another appointment, but she can still answer a few questions. In her free time, she jots down the names of young, emerging Latino artists whose performances have left a mark on her. “There’s a wave [of artists] coming out of the schools. There’s really more diversity, and they’re going to bring a wave of freshness and authenticity to what they put forward.” A pensive look crosses her face. Despite the increase in diversity, precarity in the artistic professions continues to be an issue for the children of immigrants, Carolina adds. “When your parents sacrificed everything to come to a new country, it’s hard to say ‘I’m going to go play the lottery with a job that maybe won’t pay.’”
Pour mieux refléter les réalités des com: To better reflect the realities of the communities depicted in films and series, research is essential, the screenwriter explains. “It’s our job to do what we call character work, to make a character more complex, to make them real. I learn as much as I can. If it’s based on a culture I know less about, I watch documentaries, I try to read books from that culture, to learn as much as possible in order to be… truthful.”
Près d’une semaine plus tard, Zaira Zarz: Nearly a week later, Zaira Zarza, associate professor in the Department of Art History, Film and Audiovisual Media at Université de Montréal, joins us in a Zoom session. Her short black hair frames her face and goes well with her dark brown eyes.
Dre Zaira Zarza, professeure agrégée du: Dr. Zaira Zarza, associate professor in the Department of Art History, Film and Audiovisual Media at Université de Montréal. Image courtesy of Zaira Zarza
À peine l’entrevue débutée, Zaira énumèr: Barely a minute into the interview, Zaira enthusiastically lists cinematic references: Le coyote and Les routes de février, directed by Katherine Jerkovic, who is of Uruguayan, Argentine and Croatian origin. The latter is the first Quebec film shot in Uruguay and in Spanish. Mis dos voces, by Lina Rodriguez, was filmed entirely in Canada. These three nationally acclaimed feature films are deeply rooted in the Latin Canadian life experience and showcase actresses from Latin America. “It’s this intimacy, this vulnerability [found] in [their] characters that really make their cinema, in my opinion, the most authentic, the most honest representation of the reality of immigrants, and especially of women,” says Zaira, her gaze fixed on her computer screen.
La chercheuse fait un survol de la situa: The researcher gives an overview of the situation in the United States, and can count on the fingers of one hand the Hispanic American actresses who are regularly seen on screen. “Do we see a lot of representation of women or directors of Latin American origin? No. Do we see them everywhere in the media? Are they in the mainstream? Do they have a space in Hollywood? No.” According to a study conducted in 2019 by the USC Annenberg School of 1,200 films made between 2007 and 2018, only 19 Hispanic women producers were counted. In addition, 4% of directors were Latinos. Of that total, there was only one Hispanic American woman director.
Selon Zaira, de nombreuses barrières se: According to Zaira, immigrants who want to get into this profession in a new country face many barriers. “It’s hard for people of Canadian and Quebec origin, so imagine for those whose mother tongue isn’t French or English, who don’t really know how the film system works, with SODEC, Quebecor, the National Film Board of Canada and other institutions that fund film and media. These are art forms for which funding is absolutely essential,” she reports in an empathetic tone.
Au Québec et aux États-Unis, les cinéast: In Quebec and the United States, she continues, filmmakers depend heavily on cultural funding policies. Government decisions determine whether or not screenwriters who tackle social and political subjects become visible. This is what we saw following the social struggles tied to the George Floyd and #MeToo movements, Zaira points out. “There was funding for racialized producers, for Indigenous filmmaking communities, who before had [...] very few chances of getting into the competitions. [...] But these measures continue to be cosmetic [...]: in an ideal world, this type of competition shouldn’t exist.”
Il ne reste plus que sept minutes avant: Only seven minutes remain before the platform cuts off our call. Her gaze wanders around the room where she sits, in the comfort of her home. Her eyes come to rest on our video call. For this experienced professor, one thing is clear: it all starts in school. “Every country’s cinema, in my opinion, begins with education. [If] I don’t see an Indigenous student in the classroom at Université de Montréal, no women of Latin American origin, I can imagine what will be missing from screens in the future,” she says. It is essential to attract students from various visible minority groups to the worlds of the arts, culture and media. “It’s hard, because [these] are generally very privileged, elitist careers, […] we really have to tear down that wall around the arts!”
